qs.q: Which demographic feature is characteristic of inclusion body myositis compared to other inflammatory myopathies?
o: Common among patients older than age 50 with a male-to-female ratio of 3:1
Exclusively affects female children under the age of 10 years
Typically manifests in adolescent males with acute onset over days
Shows equal gender distribution predominantly in neonates
qs.e: Inclusion body myositis is common among patients older than age 50 and has a male-to-female ratio of 3:1. Polymyositis, by contrast, is more common in women over the age of 20.

qs.q: What is considered the hallmark histological feature of inclusion body myositis?
o: Rimmed vacuoles
Caseating granulomas
Type 1 fiber predominance
Subsarcolemmal mitochondrial aggregates
qs.e: Rimmed vacuoles are the hallmark feature of inclusion body myositis on muscle biopsy. Granulomas and isolated fiber type shifts are characteristic of other pathologies.

qs.q: Which muscle groups are characteristically and early involved in inclusion body myositis?
o: Extraocular and facial muscles
Finger flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, and knee extensors
Tongue and pharyngeal constrictors exclusively
Intercostal muscles and the diaphragm
qs.e: The pattern of muscle weakness particular to IBM is early involvement of the finger flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, and knee extensors. Other options describe involvement patterns foreign to this specific diagnostic profile.

qs.q: What is a notable distinguishing clinical feature of inclusion body myositis when compared to polymyositis?
o: Acute onset with rapid recovery within weeks
Asymmetric and distal muscle involvement with insidious progression
Strictly symmetrical proximal weakness sparing all distal muscle groups
Immediate and complete response to standard high-dose corticosteroids
qs.e: IBM is unique in featuring asymmetric and distal muscle involvement along with an insidious, slowly progressive onset. Polymyositis predominantly presents with symmetric proximal weakness.

qs.q: Which antibody is specifically noted in the workup for inclusion body myositis?
o: Anti-Jo-1 antibody
Mup44 antibody
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide
Anti-centromere antibody
qs.e: The Mup44 antibody is referenced in the workup for inclusion body myositis. Anti-Jo-1 is a classic myositis-specific antibody found in other inflammatory settings.

qs.q: What is the hallmark histological feature that distinguishes inclusion body myositis from other inflammatory myopathies?
o: MHC class 1 expression on non-necrotic fibers
Perforin-positive CD8+ T cell invasion patterns
Presence of characteristic rimmed vacuoles
Scattered regenerating muscle fiber profiles
qs.e: Rimmed vacuoles are the hallmark histological feature of inclusion body myositis. While CD8+ T cell invasion and MHC class 1 expression occur in both polymyositis and inclusion body myositis, rimmed vacuoles are unique to the latter.

qs.q: Which clinical pattern of muscle involvement is unique to inclusion body myositis compared to other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies?
o: Exclusive involvement of proximal shoulder and hip
Involvement of proximal and distal musculature
Purely distal foot and hand muscle weakness
Rapidly progressive facial and extraocular weakness
qs.e: Unlike other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, inclusion body myositis is unique in that it involves both proximal and distal musculature in a symmetric or asymmetric fashion. Other myopathies largely spare distal muscles.

qs.q: Which specific muscle groups show early involvement and are characteristic of inclusion body myositis?
o: Neck flexor muscles and extraocular muscles
Finger flexors and ankle dorsiflexor muscles
Shoulder abductor and hip adductor muscles
Distal toe extensor and facial muscles
qs.e: The pattern of muscle weakness particular to inclusion body myositis is early involvement of the finger flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, and knee extensors. This leads to symptoms such as foot drop and difficulty gripping.
